# sysutils_systemd_unit (Resource)

Manages a systemd unit: writes its unit file to `/etc/systemd/system`, runs `systemctl daemon-reload` when the file changes, and optionally enables and starts or stops the unit. On destroy the unit is stopped and disabled, and its file is removed. Requires root privileges and a host booted with systemd.

Use it for units that you define yourself. To change a unit that a package installed, manage a drop-in file such as `/etc/systemd/system/ssh.service.d/override.conf` with [`sysutils_file`](./file.md) and restart the unit with the `restart_on_change` of a [`sysutils_service`](./service.md), which reloads systemd first. `sysutils_service` also manages whether units that a package installed are enabled and running.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Run a small web service as the "appsvc" user, start it now and at boot.
resource "sysutils_systemd_unit" "app" {
  name    = "app.service"
  enabled = true
  state   = "running"

  content = <<-EOT
    [Unit]
    Description=Example application
    After=network-online.target
    Wants=network-online.target

    [Service]
    User=appsvc
    ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 127.0.0.1
    Restart=on-failure

    [Install]
    WantedBy=multi-user.target
  EOT
}

# A oneshot service triggered by a timer. The service itself is neither
# enabled nor started; the timer is.
resource "sysutils_systemd_unit" "backup" {
  name   = "backup.service"
  source = "${path.module}/units/backup.service"
}

resource "sysutils_systemd_unit" "backup_timer" {
  name    = "backup.timer"
  enabled = true
  state   = "running"

  content = <<-EOT
    [Timer]
    OnCalendar=daily
    Persistent=true

    [Install]
    WantedBy=timers.target
  EOT

  # Make sure the service exists before the timer can fire.
  depends_on = [sysutils_systemd_unit.backup]
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Unit name including its type suffix, such as `"app.service"` or `"backup.timer"`. Supported suffixes are `.service`, `.socket`, `.target`, `.timer`, `.path`, `.mount`, `.automount`, `.swap` and `.slice`. Template and instance units (names containing `@`) are not supported. A unit with this name must not already exist anywhere on the host. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `content` (String) Contents of the unit file. Exactly one of `content` and `source` must be set.
- `enabled` (Boolean) Whether the unit is enabled to start at boot (`systemctl enable`/`disable`). If unset, the enablement is not managed and the current value is reported. Only units with an `[Install]` section can be enabled.
- `restart_on_change` (Boolean) Whether to restart the unit (`systemctl try-restart`) when its unit file changes and it is running, so that the change takes effect. Never applies while `state` is `"stopped"`. Defaults to `true`.
- `source` (String) Path to a local file whose contents are used as the unit file. Exactly one of `content` and `source` must be set. Relative paths are resolved against Terraform's working directory; prefer `${path.module}/...`. The source is hashed during every plan, so a change to its contents plans an update.
- `state` (String) Whether the unit should be `"running"` or `"stopped"` (`systemctl start`/`stop`). If unset, the unit is not started or stopped and the current value is reported. A unit counts as running when `systemctl is-active` reports `active`, `reloading` or `refreshing`.
- `timeout` (String) Maximum time each `systemctl` invocation may take, as a Go duration such as `"30s"` or `"5m"`. `systemctl start` and `stop` wait for the unit to finish starting or stopping, so this should exceed the unit's own start and stop timeouts. Defaults to `"2m"`.

### Read-Only

- `content_sha256` (String) Hex-encoded SHA-256 checksum of the unit file. Known at plan time, so other resources can use it to react to changes of the unit.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).
- `path` (String) Path of the unit file, `/etc/systemd/system/<name>`.

## Behavior

### Create

1. The provider refuses to create the unit if `/etc/systemd/system/<name>` already exists (import it instead), or if systemd already knows a unit of that name from anywhere else, such as a package's unit in `/usr/lib/systemd/system` or a runtime unit in `/run/systemd/system`. A file in `/etc/systemd/system` would silently override that unit, and destroying the resource would then stop and disable it.
2. The unit file is written atomically with mode `0644`, owned by the user running Terraform.
3. `systemctl daemon-reload` runs, and the provider checks that systemd could load the unit (`LoadState=loaded`). A unit with a fatal error, such as a service without `ExecStart=`, fails the apply.
4. If `enabled` is set, the unit is enabled or disabled. If `state` is set, it is started or stopped. Both are checked afterwards: enabling a unit without an `[Install]` section, or starting a unit that exits right away, is an error rather than a permanent diff.

If a step after writing the file fails, the resource is still recorded in state, marked as tainted, so the next apply replaces it and destroy cleans it up.

### Update

When the unit file content differs from the configuration, the file is replaced atomically and `systemctl daemon-reload` runs. Then:

- If the unit is enabled, it is re-enabled (`systemctl reenable`) so that changes to its `[Install]` section take effect, unless `enabled = false`.
- If the unit is running and `restart_on_change` is `true`, it is restarted with `systemctl try-restart`, unless `state = "stopped"`.

After that, `enabled` and `state` are applied as on create. Changing only `enabled`, `state`, `restart_on_change` or `timeout` does not touch the unit file and does not reload systemd.

### Destroy

The unit is stopped (or its failed state reset), disabled, and its file is removed, followed by `systemctl daemon-reload`. If the file was already deleted out of band, the unit is only stopped if systemd still has it loaded from that file. If something other than a regular file now sits at the unit's path, destroy leaves everything in place and emits a warning.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the unit file and runs `systemctl is-enabled` and `systemctl is-active`:

- A changed unit file shows up as a diff of `content`, or of `content_sha256` when `source` is used. The next apply rewrites the file, reloads systemd and restarts the unit as described above.
- `enabled` is `true` only when `systemctl is-enabled` reports `enabled`. `enabled-runtime`, `static`, `indirect`, `masked` and the like count as `false`.
- `state` is `"running"` when `systemctl is-active` reports `active`, `reloading` or `refreshing`, and `"stopped"` otherwise, including `failed` and `activating`. `systemctl start` waits until the unit has finished starting, so a unit still `activating` afterwards is typically stuck in a restart loop.
- With `enabled` or `state` unset in the configuration, the current value is recorded in state but never changed, and never shows up as a diff. When the unit file changes, they are shown as `(known after apply)`, because re-enabling or restarting the unit can change them.
- If the unit file was deleted, the resource is removed from state and the next plan recreates it.

## Timeouts

Every `systemctl` invocation is limited by `timeout` (2 minutes by default) and killed when it expires, which fails the apply. `systemctl start`, `stop` and `try-restart` wait for the unit's start or stop job, so choose a `timeout` longer than the unit's own `TimeoutStartSec=`/`TimeoutStopSec=`. A job that systemd has already accepted keeps running after `systemctl` is killed.

## Import

An existing unit file in `/etc/systemd/system` can be imported by unit name:

```shell
# By unit name; the unit file must be in /etc/systemd/system.
terraform import sysutils_systemd_unit.app app.service
```

After import, `content` holds the file's contents and `enabled` and `state` reflect the unit's current status. `restart_on_change` and `timeout` are set to their defaults.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root and a host running systemd as PID 1. It manages the system instance only, not user units (`systemctl --user`).
- Template and instance units (`foo@.service`, `foo@bar.service`) are not supported.
- A `Type=oneshot` service without `RemainAfterExit=yes` becomes inactive as soon as it has run, so `state = "running"` fails for it. Leave `state` unset for such services and start them through a timer or another unit.
- The unit file content is stored in Terraform state. Don't put secrets in `Environment=` lines; use `EnvironmentFile=` or credentials instead.
- The unit file is written atomically, but the provider does not lock `/etc/systemd/system` against other tools. A symlink at the unit's path, such as a unit masked with `systemctl mask`, is refused.
